**Q. Does SPI-3 + 3 consecutive months $≈$ SPI-6 directly? Are we doing something roundabout?**

```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
```

To assess this question, I used real SPI data calculated from ERA5 for
the six project countries (Argentina, Greece, Thailand, Mexico, South
Africa, and Benin) covering 1975–2023. I compared drought events
detected under two definitions:

- **Definition A:** SPI-3 with a 3-consecutive-month rule — a drought
  is confirmed only when SPI-3 remains below −0.5 for three consecutive
  months, and ends when SPI-3 recovers above −0.5
- **Definition B:** SPI-6 applied directly — a drought starts the
  moment SPI-6 drops below −0.5 and ends when it recovers above −0.5


(The original discussion referred to SPI-5 vs SPI-3 + 2 consecutive
months. Since SPI-5 was not calculated in our pipeline, I used the
above equivalent formulation where the core argument remains the same.)

**Key Finding: The Two Definitions Are Not Equivalent**

The following graph shows the distribution of drought events based on the two definitions described above, using the dataset outlined earlier.

![](Figures/Histogram_two_definition.png){width="60%"}

--->
The results show clearly that SPI-3 + a 3-month consecutive rule is
**not** equivalent to SPI-6 applied directly. The differences are both
numerically large and scientifically meaningful. SPI-6 detects 60%
more events than SPI-3 + rule, and the mean peak
severity differs substantially (−1.22 vs −1.69).

\newpage
**Why Does SPI-6 Detect More Events?**

The difference comes down to a fundamental distinction in how each
approach responds to precipitation variability.

**- SPI-6 — A Slowly Updating Smoothed Signal**

SPI-6 accumulates precipitation over a 6-month rolling window, meaning
consecutive monthly values share five of their six input months. Once
SPI-6 drops below −0.5 it tends to remain there for an extended period
because the window updates only gradually — each new month replaces only
one-sixth of the accumulated total:

$$
\text{SPI-6}_{t} = f(P_{t-5},\, P_{t-4},\, P_{t-3},\, P_{t-2},\, P_{t-1},\, P_{t})
$$

$$
\text{SPI-6}_{t+1} = f(\underbrace{P_{t-4},\, P_{t-3},\, P_{t-2},\, P_{t-1},\, P_{t}}_{\text{5 months shared with } t},\, P_{t+1})
$$

This high autocorrelation means SPI-6 readily flags any dip below −0.5
as a drought event, without requiring the signal to persist across
consecutive time steps.

**- SPI-3 + Rule — A Strict Persistence Filter**

SPI-3 updates faster and is more sensitive to individual months. The
3-consecutive-month rule requires SPI-3 to remain below −0.5 for three
months in a row before an event is confirmed. This filters out brief
transient dips that SPI-6 would readily flag, retaining only sustained
drought signals.

- SPI-3 updates faster → more month-to-month variability → harder to
  remain below −0.5 for three consecutive months
- SPI-6 updates slowly → strong autocorrelation → easier to remain
  below −0.5 because 5 of 6 months are shared between consecutive
  readings


**Why Do They Classify Severity Differently?**

The mean peak SPI difference (−1.69 vs −1.22) reflects the filtering
effect directly. SPI-6 captures many short mild eventsm (shallow dips
just below −0.5). The SPI-3 consecutive rule only confirms events that
have already persisted for three months, which tend to be deeper and
more genuine droughts.
<!---

--->
In practical terms the consecutive month rule acts as a quality
filter and retaining impactful drought events while discarding transient
dips that are unlikely to have meaningful agricultural consequences.


**The Role of Wet Month Interruptions**

Another important factor explaining the disagreement between the
two definitions is the prevalence of wet month interruptions: brief
above-threshold months embedded within a dry spell, before conditions
deteriorate again.

<!---
```{r interruption-stats}
#| label: tbl-interruptions
#| tbl-cap: "Wet month interruption statistics across all study pixels"

interruption_data <- data.frame(
  Metric = c(
    "Total pixels analysed",
    "Pixels with at least one interruption",
    "Percentage of pixels affected",
    "Total interruptions across all pixels"
  ),
  Value = c(
    "10,993",
    "10,942",
    "99.5%",
    "59,171"
  )
)

kable(
  interruption_data,
  align = c("l", "c"),
  booktabs = TRUE
) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width        = FALSE,
    position          = "center"
  ) %>%
  column_spec(2, bold = TRUE, color = "#185FA5")
```


This prevalence is climatologically expected given the high rainfall
variability across the study countries, driven by ENSO, the South
American Monsoon, and other regional circulation patterns. The two
definitions handle these interruptions in fundamentally different ways:
--->

**SPI-6 at a month of interruption:**
The long accumulation window means one wet month replaces only
one-sixth of the total. SPI-6 typically remains negative and treats the
entire period as **one continuous event**.

**SPI-3 + rule at a month of interruption:**
The wet month pushes SPI-3 above the threshold, breaking the
consecutive sequence and ending the first event. Three more dry months
are then required to confirm a new event. So it either
ends the first event and does not restart until 3 dry months
accumulate again — treating it as two separate events or a gap

<!---
Because wet month interruptions occur at 99.5% of pixels, the two
definitions almost always disagree on event boundaries — which explains
why pixel-level agreement is effectively zero. This is not a flaw in
either approach but reflects a genuine scientific choice about how to
handle brief recoveries within drought periods.
--->

```{r interruption-diagram}
#| label: fig-interruption
#| fig-cap: "How each definition handles wet month interruptions. SPI-6 treats the period as one continuous event. SPI-3 + rule either splits into two events (if 3 dry months follow) or misses the second event entirely (if variability prevents 3 consecutive dry months)."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 9

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

months <- 1:12

# --- Scenario 1: SPI-3 splits into two events ---
spi3_split <- c(-0.8, -0.7, 0.2, -0.9, -1.1, -0.6, -0.8, -0.9,
                0.1, -0.3, -0.2, 0.1)
spi6_split <- c(-0.3, -0.5, -0.6, -0.7, -0.9, -0.8,
                -0.7, -0.6, -0.5, -0.4, -0.3, -0.2)

# --- Scenario 2: SPI-3 misses second event ---
spi3_miss  <- c(-0.8, -0.7, 0.2, -0.9, 0.1, -0.6,
                -0.7, 0.2, -0.8, -0.3, 0.1, -0.2)
spi6_miss  <- c(-0.3, -0.5, -0.6, -0.7, -0.8, -0.7,
                -0.6, -0.5, -0.6, -0.5, -0.4, -0.3)

df_split <- data.frame(month = months,
                        spi3  = spi3_split,
                        spi6  = spi6_split)

df_miss  <- data.frame(month = months,
                        spi3  = spi3_miss,
                        spi6  = spi6_miss)

# ---- Shared theme ----
base_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 9),
    axis.text.x   = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1, size = 8)
  )

month_labels <- paste("M", months)

# ============================================================
# SCENARIO 1 — SPI-3 splits into two events
# ============================================================

p1a <- ggplot(df_split, aes(x = month)) +
  # Event 1 shading
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.5, xmax = 2.5,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#EF9A9A", alpha = 0.25) +
  # Event 2 shading
  annotate("rect", xmin = 3.5, xmax = 8.5,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#EF9A9A", alpha = 0.25) +
  # Labels
  annotate("text", x = 1.5,  y =  0.7, label = "Event 1",
           fontface = "bold", colour = "#C62828", size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 6.0,  y =  0.7, label = "Event 2",
           fontface = "bold", colour = "#C62828", size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.0,  y =  0.7,
           label = "Wet\nmonth", colour = "grey40",
           size = 2.8, fontface = "italic") +
  annotate("text", x = 9.5, y = 0.7,
           label = "No event\n(recovered)",
           colour = "grey40", size = 2.8, fontface = "italic") +
  # Reference lines
  geom_hline(yintercept =  0,   colour = "grey60",   linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -0.5, colour = "firebrick",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  # SPI line
  geom_line(aes(y = spi3), colour = "#5C9BD6", linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_point(aes(y = spi3, colour = spi3 < -0.5),
             size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "firebrick",
                                 "FALSE" = "#5C9BD6")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = months, labels = month_labels) +
  labs(
    title    = "Definition A — Scenario 1: SPI-3 + 3 month rule",
    subtitle = "Wet month breaks sequence but 3 dry months follow → two separate events detected",
    x = NULL, y = "SPI-3"
  ) +
  base_theme

p1b <- ggplot(df_split, aes(x = month)) +
  # One continuous event
  annotate("rect", xmin = 1.5, xmax = 9.5,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#EF9A9A", alpha = 0.25) +
  annotate("text", x = 5.5, y = 0.7,
           label = "One continuous event",
           fontface = "bold", colour = "#C62828", size = 3.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept =  0,   colour = "grey60",   linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -0.5, colour = "firebrick",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = spi6), colour = "#E67E22", linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_point(aes(y = spi6, colour = spi6 < -0.5),
             size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "firebrick",
                                 "FALSE" = "#E67E22")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = months, labels = month_labels) +
  labs(
    title    = "Definition B — Scenario 1: SPI-6 direct",
    subtitle = "Long memory keeps SPI-6 negative throughout → one event",
    x = NULL, y = "SPI-6"
  ) +
  base_theme

# ============================================================
# SCENARIO 2 — SPI-3 misses second event entirely
# ============================================================

p2a <- ggplot(df_miss, aes(x = month)) +
  # Only Event 1
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.5, xmax = 2.5,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#EF9A9A", alpha = 0.25) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y =  0.7, label = "Event 1",
           fontface = "bold", colour = "#C62828", size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.0, y =  0.7,
           label = "Wet\nmonth", colour = "grey40",
           size = 2.8, fontface = "italic") +
  # Arrow showing missed second event
  annotate("text", x = 7.0, y = 0.7,
           label = "No second event\n(variability prevents\n3 consecutive dry months)",
           colour = "#E53935", size = 2.8, fontface = "italic") +
  geom_hline(yintercept =  0,   colour = "grey60",   linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -0.5, colour = "firebrick",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = spi3), colour = "#5C9BD6", linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_point(aes(y = spi3, colour = spi3 < -0.5),
             size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "firebrick",
                                 "FALSE" = "#5C9BD6")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = months, labels = month_labels) +
  labs(
    title    = "Definition A — Scenario 2: SPI-3 + 3 month rule",
    subtitle = "Wet month interruptions keep resetting the counter → second event MISSED entirely",
    x = NULL, y = "SPI-3"
  ) +
  base_theme

p2b <- ggplot(df_miss, aes(x = month)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 1.5, xmax = 10.5,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#EF9A9A", alpha = 0.25) +
  annotate("text", x = 6.0, y = 0.7,
           label = "One continuous event",
           fontface = "bold", colour = "#C62828", size = 3.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept =  0,   colour = "grey60",   linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -0.5, colour = "firebrick",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = spi6), colour = "#E67E22", linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_point(aes(y = spi6, colour = spi6 < -0.5),
             size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "firebrick",
                                 "FALSE" = "#E67E22")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = months, labels = month_labels) +
  labs(
    title    = "Definition B — Scenario 2: SPI-6 direct",
    subtitle = "SPI-6 stays below threshold throughout → still detects one long event",
    x = NULL, y = "SPI-6"
  ) +
  base_theme

# ============================================================
# Combine all four panels
# ============================================================

(p1a + p1b) / (p2a + p2b) +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "How each definition handles wet month interruptions",
    caption = paste(
      "Red shading = drought event detected.",
      "Dashed line = -0.5 threshold.",
      "Scenario 2 is the more common outcome given",
      "high rainfall variability across study countries."
    ),
    theme = theme(
      plot.title   = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.caption = element_text(size = 8, colour = "grey50")
    )
  )
```
\newpage
**Bottom Line**

The consecutive month rule and a longer SPI window are doing
fundamentally different things:

- The **consecutive month rule** filters by persistence of the drought
  signal itself — it checks whether the index stays anomalous across
  subsequent time steps
- A **longer SPI window** smooths the precipitation input — it carries
  a longer memory of past conditions into each monthly value

<!---
In highly variable climates such as those in our study countries, where
wet month interruptions occur at 99.5% of pixels, these two mechanisms
produce substantially different results:

| | SPI-3 + consecutive rule | SPI-6 direct |
|--|--|--|
| Events | Fewer, more severe | More, mostly mild |
| Handles interruptions | Splits into separate events | Treats as one continuous event |
| Effective behaviour | Quality filter | Broad sensitive detector |

Rather than one being a roundabout version of the other, they represent
genuinely different scientific choices about what constitutes a drought
worth flagging. The consecutive month rule is not equivalent to using a
longer SPI window — it is doing something meaningfully different, and in
variable climates that difference matters substantially.
--->
